label: Title
notes: Open the lecture by making the scale change explicit. Earlier chapters asked for exact distances and compact limits; this chapter asks what survives when bounded errors become negligible. Frame the title question as a filter: large-scale geometry keeps the features that remain visible from far away.

label: Scale Shift
notes: Use this slide to move students from local metric control to asymptotic control. A bounded perturbation can matter intensely inside a small ball, yet disappear after rescaling. The theme is not that small-scale geometry is unimportant, but that a different equivalence relation is being used.

label: Roadmap
notes: Preview the five sections through their diagnostics rather than through definitions alone. Pointed limits inspect neighborhoods around a basepoint, cones inspect rescaled geometry, quasi-isometries compare spaces up to linear and additive distortion, hyperbolicity tests tree-likeness, and stable norms record periodic metrics at infinity.

label: Pointed Balls
notes: The cycle example is intentionally finite but noncompact in the limit. At radius four, the small cycle still wraps around and fails the interval test, while larger cycles have pointed balls that match the integer line. Students should see convergence as eventual agreement of every fixed inspection window.

label: Pointed Convergence
notes: Present the definition as a controlled matching problem. A basepoint anchors the comparison, a radius chooses the visible window, and an error tolerance allows approximate distance preservation. The order of quantifiers matters: fix the window first, then go far enough along the sequence.

label: Local Stability
notes: This diagnostic slide turns the definition into something computable. If every larger object gives the same radius-R distance matrix around the basepoint, the sequence has stabilized locally at that radius. The check is not a full proof, but it is a useful finite witness for the limiting picture.

label: Toward Cones
notes: After pointed limits, rescaling asks a complementary question: instead of increasing the object, shrink the metric so farther and farther regions fit into a fixed window. For the lattice, each scale halves the mesh and the sampled window begins to look like a continuum.

label: Scaling Formula
notes: Keep the formula simple and then say what it does. Multiplying a metric by lambda multiplies every distance, every ball radius threshold, and every covering radius by the same factor. The interesting limit comes from sending lambda toward zero while holding the display window fixed.

label: Cone Lab
notes: The lab is a visual experiment for asymptotic cones. The records show the mesh sizes 1, one half, one quarter, and one eighth, with covering radius bounds decreasing in lockstep. Invite students to predict the next bound before revealing why the plane is the expected limit shape.

label: Quasi-Isometries
notes: Quasi-isometry is the chapter's coarse equivalence relation. Exact equality of distances is replaced by multiplicative and additive control, and a coarse-surjectivity condition prevents the target from having unseen regions. Emphasize that bounded local damage is allowed because the theory studies the far field.

label: Nets And Growth
notes: Nets are the bridge from arbitrary large-scale spaces to countable models. The growth comparison on this slide separates one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and branching behavior. The free-group tree grows explosively by radius twelve, while the lattice table behaves quadratically.

label: Z2 Into R2
notes: Use the inclusion of the l1 lattice into Euclidean space as a concrete inequality check. The sampled lambda is square root of two and the additive constant is zero, so the lower and upper inequalities hold on all sampled pairs. This is an approachable quasi-isometry before the abstract examples.

label: Hyperbolicity
notes: The tree-like diagnostic should be explained before the word hyperbolic becomes formal. In a tree, geodesic triangles are forced through shared branches; in grids and cycles, rectangles and loops create thick triangles. Hyperbolicity measures how large that thickness must be.

label: Residuals
notes: This slide gives numerical evidence for the diagnostic. The binary tree has four-point delta zero and thin-triangle residual zero, while the six-by-six grid and the 24-cycle have residuals five and six. Stress that the witnesses locate where the tree model breaks.

label: Periodic Metrics
notes: Periodic metrics are where discrete local rules become a norm at large scale. The generator costs produce a finite rulebook on the lattice, but after many steps the distance per unit displacement stabilizes. The stable norm is the macroscopic shadow of that periodic rulebook.

label: Stable Unit Ball
notes: The stable unit ball is both a shape and a growth signal. The recorded area is about 2.493, and the lattice ball count divided by radius squared stays close to the same value. This is the visual moment where periodic distance, asymptotic norm, and counting data align.

label: Recap
notes: Close by returning to the lecture question. Pointed limits, cones, quasi-isometries, hyperbolicity, and stable norms are all answers to what remains visible at infinity. The final exercise asks students to move among those viewpoints instead of treating the definitions as separate islands.
